subject: Behavior based path simulation using ctmm

messages.author: bd4368f44a7010d6
messages.subject: Behavior based path simulation using ctmm
parts:
Hey Chris,


Within my study I tried to simulate White Storks movement path of different behavioral clusters (consecutive locations of the same behavioral class). I need to do this in order to derive the time spent in certain areas of interest during a specific activity. For that purpose, I followed the steps discussed with you during the AniMove 2017 using a test data set of one individual. The data was captured during breeding season (April to August) with a default temporal interval of 5 mins which is, due to bad weather conditions, sometimes decreased to 20 minutes or even one hour intervals. Furthermore, every night, the device shuts down for 6 hours between around 8pm and 2am. In the following, the applied steps are explained in detail:


a) Derivation of behavioral clusters (each behavioral cluster should at least contain 5 consecutive locations)


Data$Behavior_Clust


b) Mean centering of behavioral clusters: The mean x and mean y location of all points of a clusterx are subtracted from each x and y point-location of a clusterx


library(tidyverse)

Bouts_centered ← Data %>%

group_by(Behavior_Clust) %>%

mutate(location.long_centered = location.long – mean(location.long)

(location.lat_centered = location.lat – mean(locationlat)


Remark: I did the mean centering using WGS84 coordinates (latitude, longitude), replacing the initial location.long and location.lat by location.long_centered and location.lat_centered


c) Conversion of mean centered behavioral clusters (WGS84) to a telemetry object with ETRS89 projection.


Bouts_centered_Tele <- as.telemetry(Bouts_centered, timezone ="UTC", timeformat= "%F %T",

projection = CRS("+init=epsg:3035"))


Subsequently, I created a variogram() and visually derived the initial GUESS parameters (accounting for irregular sampling intervals of 5,10 & 20 minutes)


dt <- c(5,10,20) %#% "minutes"

# confidence intervals

level <- c(0.5,0.95) # 50% and 95% CIs

# create Variogram

#--> accounting for irregular sampling schemes

VAR_irr <- variogram(Bouts_centered_Tele, dt=dt, res = 2)

# Variogram fitting

variogram.fit(VAR_irr, name = 'GUESS_VAR_irr', fast =F)


d) Selection of candidate ctmm’s using ctmm.select()


# Error estimate (see Question 2)

GUESS_VAR_irr$error <- 5

# control <- list(method='pNewton',cores=2)

FIT_5 <- ctmm.select(Bouts_centered_Tele, GUESS_VAR_irr, control=control, trace=TRUE,

verbose = TRUE)


e) Derivation of fitted ctmm per behavioral cluster


### Derive mean of x & y ETRS89 coordinates of each behavioral cluster:


Convert WGS84 (location.long,location.lat) to ETRS (X, Y)

Data_projected ← sptransform()


# Derive Mean

Bouts_location_mean <- Data_projected %>%

group_by(Behavior_Clust) %>%

summarise(x_mean = mean(X),

y_mean = mean(Y)) %>%

data.frame()


### Create a function which adds the means (x_mean & y_mean) of each behavioral cluster to the maximum likelihood stationary mean vector estimate (FIT_5$mu) of the FIT_5 object


FitPerBout <- function(Bouts_location_mean,FIT){

# select model with best fit (lowest dAICc) = first model in the list of candidate models

FIT_sub <- FIT[[1]]

# add mean of x and y positions per bout to FIT$mu

FIT_sub$mu[1,1] <- FIT_sub$mu[1,1] + mean(Bouts_location_mean$x_mean)

FIT_sub$mu[1,2] <- FIT_sub$mu[1,2] + mean(Bouts_location_mean$y_mean)

return(FIT_sub)

}


### lapply FitPerBout() function


Bout_FITS <- lapply(unique(Bouts_location_mean$Behavior_Clust), function(x)

{FitPerBout(Bouts_location_mean[Bouts_location_mean$ Behavior_Clust %in% x,], FIT = FIT_5)})

# name fits according to bouts

names(Bout_FITS) <- paste0('Bout_',unique(Bouts_location_mean$Behavior_Clust))


f) Simulation of n trajectories per behavioral cluster


Simulated_Paths <- lapply(unique(Stork_Bouts$Behavior_Clust), function(i){

# convert behavioral cluster to Telemetry object

TeleObject <- ctmm::as.telemetry(object = Stork_Bouts[Stork_Bouts$Behavior_Clust %in% i,],timezone ="UTC", timeformat= "%F %T",

projection = CRS("+init=epsg:3035")) # ETRS89

# simulate trajectories per behavioral cluster and add them to a list

n <- 5 # n = number of simulations

CSIMS <- lapply(1:n, function(r) {simulate(TeleObject,CTMM=Bout_FITS[[paste0('Bout_',i)]],res=120)}) #res = 120 (times per hour) = 30 second interval

})


Here are my questions regarding the applied approach:


Question 1) Behavior based model fitting approach


The behavior-based approach somehow works, at least in the sense that some simulated paths are the outcome. However, they seem really out of place.

Plotting the simulated paths on top of the initial locations of one behavioral cluster of the test individual (see Fig_1) revealed that the recorded locations (red points) occupy a way smaller extent than the locations of the simulated paths (black crosses). Furthermore, the locations of the simulated paths (black crosses) are not going directly through the recorded locations (red) but only run close to them (see Fig_2). Especially the latter case seems to be an indication that something has gone completely wrong, right?

In preparation for the behavior based approach, I did some path simulations using a movement model fitted to the whole, not mean-centered dataset of the test stork (covering 5 months during breeding season). Using this model, the resulting simulations (using the same points used for simulation with the behavior based approach) looked, still not perfect, but way more ‘accurate’. They were on the one hand running trough each of the original recorded locations (see Fig_8) and on the other did not occupy an exorbitantly larger extent than the original recorded locations (see Fig_7), although the selected movement model did not really fit well to the data (see Fig_5 & Fig_6).

My questions are now the following:

It seems I have done something wrong in the behavior-based approach described above. The visual fit of the movement models to the mean centered behavior clusters (spanning the whole breeding season) doesn’t look perfect. Neither in the short term nor in the long term regime (see Fig_3 and Fig_4 respectively). I tried to fit mainly to short term but there is a bump which I couldn’t fit properly (see Fig_3). Furthermore, with regard to the long term regime, there seems to be a sudden decrease in semivariance after 3.5 months (see Fig_4).

Do you have any idea how I can fix the approach in order to get a realistic and correct outcome? I will sent you the script, the data of my test individual as well as the fit objects I created. I am clueless about what has gone wrong (mixing of projections, fitting, coding?) and how to improve the outcome.


Question 2) Error estimation


Since I am using data initially collected for another study, I do not have access to a calibration file. I’ve contacted the data owner and he agreed on the fact that the ‘eobs.horizontal.accuracy.estimate’ is not a trustworthy source for error estimation. However, he could just give me a guess on the extent of the deviations from the real position of the animals. He said that he did some kind of validation in the sense that he figured out that 50% of the recorded locations, of around 4 of the 25 individuals, are within 3.6 m from the true location. Based on that he suggested me to use a rough estimate of 5 meters for the errors. Right now, he cannot access the calibration data but can look at a later point in time. Nevertheless, its not clear yet whether I will have access to it at some point. My question is thus, is the 5 meter estimate a sufficient approach or do you have any other idea? According to you vignette on dealing with errors, an initial estimate is the ‘last resort’.


Question 3) ctmm Model fitting approaches in general


I am not sure whether I should do the fitting based on the 1) whole dataset (temporally covering the breeding season), 2) daily snippets of the data 3) or based on 3) the behavior based approach described above? After we have discussed the approach further movement models, like the central place foraging, have been added to the ctmm package. Does that change anything?

Furthermore, when using the approach 1), I still have a ~6 hour time lag every night. Does that somehow influence the model in a, for my purpose (deriving the time spent in a certain area) relevant way?


These are a lot of descriptions and questions. I hope I was clear and that you can find the time and help me solving the issues encountered. Thank you very much in advance.


Best regards,

Ines

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Behavior based path simulation using ctmm
parts:
Hi Ines,

Just from first pass:

1) Fig. 1 looks crazy. If you put all the foraging data together before fitting the model and ran simulations from that model, the variance of the simulations should not dwarf the variance of the collective foraging data, so I would assume something has gone wrong here. Figs. 1&2 should be tighter to the data than Figs. 7&8. The y-axis on Figs. 3&4 is 100x smaller than the y-axis on Figs.5&6, which makes sense, but this should lead to the first simulations being 10x tighter to the clusters.

In other situations, where things look more reasonable, during the larger gaps, the simulation will become less correlated to the data and more similar to the Gaussian model. With the occurrence distribution (?occurrence) there are arguments dt.max and cor.min that you can use to avoid completely filling in gaps that are too large (otherwise you just get a big blob). Its not documented, but these arguments (dt.max and cor.min) also work on the conditional simulations. So you could run simulate() with argument dt.max=5 %#% 'min' and this would only simulate trajectories but so far out from the data, only completely filling in gaps of 5 minutes. You aren't to the point where you need to worry about this nuance, though.

With the simulations not exactly running through the data, this is appropriate if the model contains error. Then the sampled locations are taken to be erroneous and the degree to which the simulations converge on the data is determined by the size of the errors. If you set error=FALSE, then the simulations should go exactly through the data. Fig. 2 looks crazy, though, and I assume something else has gone wrong here.

2) e-obs data should be imported and calibrated from Scott LaPoint's calibration data. If you have your own calibration data from the same model tags, that would likely be preferable. With Scott's calibration data, I found the e-obs error estimates to be highly predictive, but the calibration constants were not consistent on collars that did not perform well.

Because the e-obs data get calibrated by as.telemetry (assuming everything went well) your error<-5 command doesn't do anything different from error<-TRUE, as the data already contain error variances that do not need to be fit. Overwriting the calibration requires using uere()<- on the data, but be careful to note that this is telling you how to interpret the e-obs error estimates (I treat them as an HDOP value) and not setting all error standard deviations to 5 meters, which would also require deleting the HDOP column. Some of these details are covered in vignette('error').

3) I would fit, either to the mean detrended foraging data or to the individual foraging periods depending on whether or not you can assume the foraging behavior to be homogeneous and whether or not you have sufficient data per foraging event. Either way should get you something much tighter and more appropriate than fitting to the entire dataset without detrending.

I am in the middle of coding up some models that fit better with tiny tracks and can update you when I have that working. I will not have true CPF models for some time.

Regarding the 6 hour gap at night, I would probably skip the gaps that large with the arguments I mentioned above.

I'll try to look into this more carefully in a few days or so. I am in the middle of coding and grant preparation right now.

Best,
Chris

messages.author: bd4368f44a7010d6
messages.subject: Re: Behavior based path simulation using ctmm
parts:
Hey Chris,


thank you very much again for your quick response and helpful comments. I’ve continued working on my data following your suggestions and have some follow up questions:


1 & 3) I think I solved the ‘crazy thing’ that happened when using the approach based on the foraging clusters. It was just a problem of my centered mean locations being messed up and in the wrong projection. Now that I fixed this, I got my new simulations, as you said, being tighter to the data compared to that using a model fitted on the whole data set. I also included the dt.max in my simulations, thanks for that hint, too. (see the two simulation plots in the attachment)


2) ‘e-obs data should be imported and calibrated from Scott LaPoint's calibration data’ Just to be clear, that is automatically done when converting the data to a telemetry object, right? Or do I have to do this by myself in a separate step?

‘If you have your own calibration data from the same model tags, that would likely be preferable’

As I mentioned, the data is not mine and thus I have to wait if the owner can actually find those data.

I followed the vignette on telemetry error and could not find any different approach from that done so far. As I said, the approach dealing with the errors, somehow depends on the data owners answer.

However, I was wondering, if you know a way of finding out which of the eobs-devices did not work properly? Or is that also something I will only know when I have access to a calibration file?


4) New Questions:


Now that I have my workflow for the simulations ready, I tried to figure out a proper way on how to validate and improve the ‘selected’ model for my purpose. In the variogram vignette you write that this should be done visually looking at the selected model plotted on top of the variogram as well as by evaluating the parameters resulting from summary().


4.1 Visual validation


To be honest, for me it doesn’t look like the selected model (OUF anisotropic error) does really fit the data?

When visually fitting to my data, I mainly did it for shorter time periods (up to 3 hours lag). For that time regime the fit, at least for the GUESS parameters, looked good. Nevertheless, for the longer periods it was bad, running at a way to high semivariance. However, plotting the resulting model on top of the variogram, it doesn’t look like a good fit in the short term regime (see figures timelag_minutes & timelag_hours) but only in the long term(see figure timelag months (fraction 80%)) could be achieved. Do you know what I can do to somehow improve the fit for short term because that is important for the foraging bouts, right? I still have that bump between 0.5 and 4 hours timelag. Do you know what can be causing this, because it seems to be the reason for the bad fit in that regime.

I tried the fast = F option when deriving the variogram(). However, that just makes my memory (16GBs) become full and leads to R throwing the error message: cannot allocate vector of size x. So the only way to circumvent that would be to fit to smaller portions of the data. Is that a valid approach for my purpose, not fitting with the whole dataset but stepwise? Any ideas, on improving the fit are welcome.


4.2 Validation based on numbers


Using the summary() function on the fitted models gives me the AIC and the DOF. I was browsing through papers/vignettes/ctmm manual and could only find an explanation for the AIC but not for the Degree of Freedom. What do the mean-, area and speed DOF parameters exactly describe? I am not sure. Below you see the outcomes of my ctmm.select-favored models. Can you in just a few words explain me what is important to look at when validating the model?


> summary(FITwithError)
                         dAICc DOF[mean] method
OUF anisotropic error    0.000  2461.350     ML
OUF isotropic error   4189.268  2464.922     ML

> summary(FITwithError$`OUF anisotropic error`)
$`DOF`
    mean     area    speed 
2461.350 4103.633 2059.625 

$CI
                             low        ML      high
area (hectares)        41.292072 42.585148 43.897882
tau position (minutes) 18.858180 19.704059 20.587879
tau velocity (minutes)  1.314992  1.407472  1.506456
speed (kilometers/day) 60.829615 62.172281 63.514550

4.3) Apart from the model fitting, I need to derive behavior based movement paths for 25 individuals for my study. Is it more reliable to visually fit every single one independently? I mean, it seems to be a bit of work but not completely unmanageable. Or is variogram pooling here the better way to go? 

Sorry, I know that you are quite busy right now, but I would be really happy if you find some time to answer my follow-up questions in one of these days. Thank you very, very much.

Best,
Ines

Hi Ines,

2) e-obs and ARGOS data should be automatically calibrated during as.telemetry(). The trend I found with Scott's calibration data was that e-obs devices that were missing many fixes had a much smaller UERE.

4.1) The second (higher resolution?) variogram plot looks possibly okay to me. For your analysis, you just want the first few lags to match (up to how large of gaps you will simulate through). If the sampling is irregular, you might consider bumping up the res argument until the variogram stops changing, or using fast=FALSE. This decreases some of the distortion from irregular sampling, but its not possible to remove all of it.  Remaining distortion you can examine by simulating tracks under the same irregular sampling schedule and looking at their resulting variograms.

4.2) How much IID data your autocorrelated data is worth for estimating the mean, the home-range area, and the RMS speed.

4.3) I recommend doing everything manually like you have for the first animal, and then automating (interactive=FALSE in ctmm.guess) everything in a way that saves the comparison plots to look over at the end. For 25 animals, I don't think 25 plots would be terrible to look at.

Best,
Chris
